reminder: A simple function is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) that takes only finitely many values.
definition: A [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $s\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $X$ is simple when its set of values is a [finite set](c:finite-set). Equivalently, $s=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\mathbf 1_{A_i}$ with real numbers $a_i$ and [measurable sets](c:measurable-set) $A_i$, where $\mathbf 1_{A}$ is $1$ on $A$ and $0$ elsewhere.
examples: The function $\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, with value $1$ on $[0,1]$ and $0$ elsewhere.
The function $2\cdot\mathbf 1_{[0,1)}+5\cdot\mathbf 1_{[1,3)}$ takes only the values $0$, $2$ and $5$.
Non-example: $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ is measurable but takes infinitely many values.

steps: Take a measurable function $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$.
Add the condition that $f$ takes only finitely many values.
A function that meets this condition is a simple function.
links.why: Every fact about measurable functions holds for simple functions, which are the first step in the construction of the integral.

steps: A step function takes a constant value on each of finitely many intervals.
Each interval is a measurable set.
So a step function is measurable with finitely many values, and it is a simple function.
links.why: A result for simple functions covers step functions at once.

reminder: A simple group is a nontrivial [group](c:group) whose only [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup) are the trivial subgroup and the whole group.
definition: A [group](c:group) $G$ is simple when $G$ is not the [trivial group](c:trivial-group) and every [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$ is $\{1\}$ or $G$. Equivalently, $G\ne1$ and every [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) out of $G$ is injective or trivial.
examples: The cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/p$ of prime order $p$ is simple, since its only subgroups are $\{0\}$ and the whole group.
The alternating group $A_5$ of order $60$ is simple, and it is the smallest non-abelian simple group.
Non-example: $S_3$ is not simple, because the subgroup $A_3$ of order $3$ is a normal subgroup that is neither trivial nor all of $S_3$.
Non-example: the trivial group is not simple, because a simple group must be nontrivial.

steps: A finite simple group is a finite group $G\ne1$ whose only normal subgroups are $\{1\}$ and $G$.
The finiteness of $G$ is an extra condition on top of simplicity.
Drop this condition, and the remaining definition is that of a simple group.
links.why: A fact about all simple groups applies to every finite simple group in the classification.

reminder: A simplicial complex is a set of [simplices](c:simplex) that contains all [faces](c:face) of its simplices and meets only along shared faces.
definition: A geometric simplicial complex is a set $K$ of [simplices](c:simplex) in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that every [face](c:face) of a simplex of $K$ is in $K$, and any two simplices of $K$ meet in a common face or not at all. The abstract version is a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) $K$ of nonempty [finite sets](c:finite-set) such that every nonempty subset of a member of $K$ is a member of $K$.
examples: The boundary of a triangle: three vertices and three edges, with no $2$-dimensional face.
A solid triangle together with its three edges and three vertices.
Non-example: two segments that cross at an interior point of each do not form a complex, because their intersection is not a face of either segment.
Non-example: a solid triangle without its edges is not a complex, because it misses its faces.

steps: Take a simple graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$.
Form the family of all sets $\{v\}$ with $v\in V$ and all sets $\{u,v\}$ with $uv\in E$.
This family contains every nonempty subset of each member, so it is a simplicial complex of dimension at most $1$.
links.why: A graph is the one-dimensional case, so results about complexes apply to graphs.

steps: Choose a total order on the vertex set of the complex $K$.
Let the $n$-simplices be the lists $v_0\le\dots\le v_n$ of vertices whose underlying set is a member of $K$.
Delete one entry to get a face map, and repeat one entry to get a degeneracy map.
These maps satisfy the simplicial identities, so the data form a simplicial set.
links.why: Tools for simplicial sets apply to a complex once its vertices are ordered.

reminder: A smooth map between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) has continuous [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) of every order in local coordinates.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f\colon M\to N$ between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) is smooth when, in every pair of charts, its coordinate expression has continuous [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) of all orders. For $M=\mathbb{R}^m$ and $N=\mathbb{R}^n$, this means that $f$ is of class $C^\infty$.
examples: Every polynomial map $\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ is smooth.
The exponential map $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ and the inclusion $S^1\to\mathbb{R}^2$ are smooth.
Non-example: $x\mapsto|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is continuous but has no derivative at $0$, so it is not smooth.

steps: Take a differentiable function $f$.
Require that its derivative $f'$ is differentiable too.
Repeat this for the derivatives of every order, and call the result a smooth map.
links.why: Smooth maps follow every rule for differentiable functions, such as the chain rule.

steps: A smooth function on a smooth manifold $M$ is a function $M\to\mathbb{R}$ with derivatives of all orders.
The line $\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth manifold.
So a smooth function is a smooth map into $\mathbb{R}$.
links.why: Results about smooth maps cover smooth functions as the case with target $\mathbb{R}$.

reminder: The Sobolev space $W^{k,p}$ holds the functions in $L^p$ whose weak derivatives up to order $k$ also lie in $L^p$.
definition: Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be an [open set](c:open-set), $k\ge0$ an integer and $1\le p\le\infty$. The Sobolev space $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is the set of functions $u$ in the [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^p(\Omega)$ whose [weak derivatives](c:derivative-of-a-distribution) $D^\alpha u$ with $|\alpha|\le k$ exist as [distributions](c:distribution) given by functions in $L^p(\Omega)$. For $p<\infty$ its norm is $\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}=\big(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p}^p\big)^{1/p}$.
examples: The space $W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ holds the $L^2$ functions whose gradient is also in $L^2$.
On $(-1,1)$ the function $|x|$ lies in $W^{1,p}$ for every $p$, with weak derivative $\operatorname{sign}(x)$.
Non-example: $\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is in $L^p$ but not in $W^{1,p}$, because its distributional derivative is a difference of two Dirac masses, not a function.

steps: Set $k=0$ in the definition of $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$.
Then only the multi-index $\alpha=0$ occurs, so no derivative appears.
The norm becomes the $L^p$ norm, so $W^{0,p}(\Omega)=L^p(\Omega)$.
links.why: Facts about Sobolev spaces include the facts about $L^p$ spaces as the case of no derivatives.

steps: For $p<\infty$, the map $u\mapsto\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}$ is a norm on $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$.
Take a Cauchy sequence $(u_j)$ for this norm.
Each $D^\alpha u_j$ is Cauchy in $L^p$, so it converges to a limit $v_\alpha$.
The limit $u$ of $(u_j)$ in $L^p$ has weak derivative $v_\alpha$, so $u_j\to u$ in $W^{k,p}$.
links.why: A Sobolev space is complete, so the tools for Banach spaces apply to it.

reminder: A statistic is sufficient when the [conditional distribution](c:conditional-distribution) of the data given the statistic does not depend on the parameter.
definition: Let $X$ be a [random variable](c:random-variable) whose [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $P_\theta$ depends on an unknown parameter $\theta$. A [statistic](c:statistic) $T(X)$ is sufficient for $\theta$ when the [conditional distribution](c:conditional-distribution) of $X$ given $T(X)=t$ is the same for every $\theta$. For a family with densities, this holds exactly when $p_\theta(x)=g_\theta(T(x))\,h(x)$ for some functions $g_\theta$ and $h$.
examples: For independent Bernoulli($\theta$) trials $X_1,\dots,X_n$, the sum $\sum_i X_i$ is sufficient for $\theta$.
For normal data with a known variance, the sample mean is sufficient for the mean.
Non-example: for two Bernoulli($\theta$) trials, $X_1$ alone is not sufficient, because the conditional distribution of $(X_1,X_2)$ given $X_1$ still depends on $\theta$ through $X_2$.

steps: Take a statistic $T$, which is a function of the data $X$.
Compute the conditional distribution of $X$ given $T(X)$.
If it is the same for every parameter value $\theta$, the statistic is sufficient.
links.why: A sufficient statistic is a statistic that loses no information about the parameter.

reminder: A weighted mean of numbers is the sum of each number times its weight, divided by the sum of the weights.
definition: For [real numbers](c:real-number) $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and nonnegative weights $w_1,\dots,w_n$ that do not all vanish, the weighted mean is $\sum_{i=1}^n w_ix_i\big/\sum_{i=1}^n w_i$. For positive $x_i$, the weighted geometric or harmonic mean averages $\ln x_i$ or $1/x_i$ with the same weights and then applies the inverse function.
examples: With weights $1$ and $3$, the weighted mean of $2$ and $6$ is $(1\cdot2+3\cdot6)/4=5$.
With equal weights, the weighted mean is the usual arithmetic mean.
Non-example: the weighted sum $\sum_i w_ix_i$ is not a weighted mean when the weights do not add up to $1$, because it can lie outside the range of the $x_i$.

steps: Divide each weight $w_i$ by the total $W=\sum_j w_j$ to get coefficients $c_i=w_i/W$.
The coefficients are nonnegative and add up to $1$.
The weighted mean is the linear combination $\sum_i c_ix_i$ with these coefficients.
links.why: A weighted mean follows the algebra of linear combinations, and its extra conditions keep it between the smallest and the largest value.

reminder: A [series](c:series) converges absolutely when the series of the [absolute values](c:absolute-value) of its terms converges.
definition: A [series](c:series) $\sum a_n$ of real or complex numbers converges absolutely when the series $\sum|a_n|$ of [absolute values](c:absolute-value) converges. Then the series itself [converges](c:convergence), and every rearrangement of its terms has the same sum.
examples: The series $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^n/n^2$ converges absolutely, because $\sum 1/n^2$ converges.
The geometric series $\sum_{n\ge0}2^{-n}$ converges absolutely.
Non-example: the alternating harmonic series $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}/n$ converges but not absolutely, because $\sum 1/n$ diverges.

steps: Take a series $\sum a_n$ such that $\sum|a_n|$ converges.
Its partial sums are Cauchy, because the tails of $\sum|a_n|$ tend to $0$.
In $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ every Cauchy sequence converges, so the series converges.
links.why: Absolute convergence gives a test for convergence that ignores the signs of the terms.

reminder: An algebraic surface is an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) of dimension two.
definition: An algebraic surface is an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) $S$ of dimension $2$ over a [field](c:field) $k$, often $\mathbb{C}$. For irreducible $S$, this means that the function field of $S$ has transcendence degree $2$ over $k$. Over $\mathbb{C}$, the smooth points of $S$ form a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) of complex dimension $2$.
examples: The projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2$.
A smooth cubic surface in $\mathbb{P}^3$, the zero set of a cubic form in four variables.
Non-example: the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$ is a variety of dimension $1$, so it is a curve and not a surface.

steps: Take an algebraic variety $X$ over a field $k$.
Find its dimension, which is the transcendence degree of its function field when $X$ is irreducible.
If the dimension is $2$, then $X$ is an algebraic surface.
links.why: Every fact about varieties holds for surfaces, and the dimension condition adds the tools of surface theory.

reminder: An algebraic variety is a space glued from common zero sets of polynomials over an algebraically closed field.
definition: An affine variety over an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) $k$ is the common zero set in $k^n$ of a family of [polynomials](c:polynomial), with the Zariski topology, whose closed sets are such zero sets. An algebraic variety is a [topological space](c:topological-space) with a sheaf of functions that is a finite union of open pieces, each an affine variety, and that is separated.
examples: The parabola $y=x^2$ in the plane $k^2$.
Projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$, covered by $n+1$ copies of $k^n$.
Non-example: the graph of $y=\sin x$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$ is not an algebraic variety, because $\sin$ is not a polynomial.
Non-example: the affine line with a doubled origin, glued from two copies of $k$ along $k\setminus\{0\}$, is not separated, so it is not a variety.

steps: Cover the variety $X$ by affine varieties with coordinate rings $A_i$.
Replace each piece by its prime spectrum $\operatorname{Spec}A_i$, and glue along the same overlaps.
The result is a scheme, and it remembers $X$ through its closed points.
This scheme is reduced, separated and of finite type over $k$.
links.why: A variety is a scheme with extra conditions, so scheme theory applies to varieties.

steps: Take a projective variety $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^n$, the zero set of homogeneous polynomials.
It is covered by the $n+1$ affine pieces $X\cap\{x_i\ne0\}$.
Each piece is an affine variety, so $X$ is a variety in the general sense.
links.why: Results for varieties apply to projective varieties, which are the varieties that sit closed in a projective space.

reminder: A Banach algebra is an associative algebra with a complete norm that satisfies $\|xy\|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$.
definition: A Banach algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ is an associative [algebra over a field](c:algebra-over-a-field) $A$ with a [norm](c:norm) such that $A$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space) and $\|xy\|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for all $x,y\in A$. This inequality makes the multiplication continuous. Many authors also require a unit $1$ with $\|1\|=1$.
examples: The algebra $C(K)$ of complex continuous functions on a compact space $K$, with the supremum norm.
The algebra of bounded operators on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), with the operator norm.
Non-example: the algebra of polynomials on $[0,1]$ with the supremum norm has a submultiplicative norm but is not complete.

steps: Start with a Banach space $A$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
Add an associative bilinear multiplication $A\times A\to A$.
Require $\|xy\|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so that the multiplication fits the norm.
links.why: Every fact about Banach spaces, such as arguments that use completeness, applies to a Banach algebra.

steps: A C*-algebra is a Banach algebra $A$ with an involution $x\mapsto x^*$.
The involution satisfies $\|x^*x\|=\|x\|^2$ for all $x$.
Forget the involution, and $A$ is still a Banach algebra.
links.why: Results for Banach algebras, such as formulas for the spectral radius, apply to every C*-algebra.

reminder: A function into a [metric space](c:metric-space) is bounded when its [image](c:image) lies in some ball of finite radius.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f\colon X\to Y$ into a [metric space](c:metric-space) $Y$ is bounded when its [image](c:image) $f(X)$ is a bounded set. That is, there are $y_0\in Y$ and $R<\infty$ with $d(f(x),y_0)\le R$ for all $x\in X$. For real-valued $f$, this means $|f(x)|\le M$ for all $x$ and some $M$.
examples: The function $\sin\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is bounded, since $|\sin x|\le1$.
Every continuous function from a compact space to $\mathbb{R}$ is bounded, for example $x^2$ on $[0,1]$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto1/x$ on $(0,1]$ is not bounded, because its values grow without limit as $x\to0$.

steps: Take a bounded continuous function $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ on a topological space $X$.
Its image is a bounded set, so $f$ is a bounded function.
Conversely, a bounded function is a bounded continuous function exactly when it is also continuous.
links.why: Bounds proved for bounded functions hold for bounded continuous functions.

reminder: The chromatic number of a [graph](c:graph) is the least number of colors that gives adjacent vertices different colors.
definition: The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is the smallest $k$ such that $G$ has a proper $k$-[coloring](c:graph-coloring). A proper $k$-coloring is a map $c\colon V(G)\to\{1,\dots,k\}$ with $c(u)\ne c(v)$ whenever $u$ and $v$ are joined by an edge.
examples: For the complete graph $K_n$ on $n$ vertices, $\chi(K_n)=n$.
For a cycle, $\chi(C_n)=2$ when $n$ is even and $\chi(C_n)=3$ when $n$ is odd.
Non-example: giving the two ends of an edge the same color is not a proper coloring, so it does not count.

reminder: A competitive equilibrium is a price vector and an allocation where every agent picks a best affordable bundle and all markets clear.
definition: In an exchange economy with agents $i=1,\dots,m$ and endowments $e_i$, a competitive equilibrium is a price vector $p$ and an allocation $(x_i)$ such that each $x_i$ is a most preferred bundle of agent $i$, by the [preferences](c:preference-relation) of $i$, among the bundles $x$ with $p\cdot x\le p\cdot e_i$. In addition, supply meets demand in every market: $\sum_i x_i=\sum_i e_i$.
examples: In an Edgeworth box with two agents and two goods, a price ratio at which the two offer curves cross gives a competitive equilibrium.
If no agent wants to trade at some prices, then the initial endowments together with those prices form an equilibrium.
Non-example: prices at which the total demand for one good exceeds its total endowment do not clear that market, so they are not equilibrium prices.

reminder: A complex number has the form $a+bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are [real numbers](c:real-number) and $i^2=-1$.
definition: The complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ are the pairs of [real numbers](c:real-number), written $a+bi$, with addition $(a+bi)+(c+di)=(a+c)+(b+d)i$ and multiplication $(a+bi)(c+di)=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i$. With these operations $\mathbb{C}$ is a [field](c:field) that contains $\mathbb{R}$ and an element $i$ with $i^2=-1$.
examples: The number $3+4i$ has real part $3$, imaginary part $4$ and modulus $5$.
The square of $1+i$ is $(1+i)^2=2i$.
Non-example: the set $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the componentwise product $(a,b)(c,d)=(ac,bd)$ is not the complex numbers, because it has zero divisors such as $(1,0)(0,1)=(0,0)$.

steps: Send each real number $a$ to the complex number $a+0i$.
This map keeps sums and products, since $(a+0i)(b+0i)=ab+0i$ and $(a+0i)+(b+0i)=(a+b)+0i$.
So the real numbers are exactly the complex numbers with imaginary part $0$.
links.why: Every statement about complex numbers also holds for real numbers, which are the complex numbers with imaginary part zero.

reminder: A formal theory is consistent when no [deduction](c:deduction) in it proves a [contradiction](c:contradiction).
definition: A formal theory $T$ is consistent when there is no [deduction](c:deduction) in $T$ of a [contradiction](c:contradiction), that is, $T\nvdash\bot$. In classical logic this holds exactly when there is no sentence $\varphi$ such that $T$ proves both $\varphi$ and $\neg\varphi$. A theory that is not consistent is [inconsistent](c:inconsistency).
examples: A theory that has a model, such as the axioms of a group, is consistent.
The first-order theory with no axioms is consistent.
Non-example: the theory with the two axioms $P$ and $\neg P$ is inconsistent, because it proves $P\wedge\neg P$.

reminder: An equivalence of categories is a [functor](c:functor) with an inverse functor up to [natural isomorphism](c:natural-isomorphism).
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F\colon C\to D$ between [categories](c:category) is an equivalence when there is a functor $G\colon D\to C$ with [natural isomorphisms](c:natural-isomorphism) $GF\cong\mathrm{id}_C$ and $FG\cong\mathrm{id}_D$. With the axiom of choice, this holds exactly when $F$ is fully faithful and every object of $D$ is [isomorphic](c:isomorphism) to $F(c)$ for some object $c$ of $C$.
examples: The category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over $k$ is equivalent to the category whose objects are $0,1,2,\dots$ and whose morphisms are matrices over $k$.
The inclusion of a skeleton of a category $C$ into $C$ is an equivalence.
Non-example: the forgetful functor from groups to sets is not an equivalence, because it is not full, as most functions between groups are not homomorphisms.

steps: Take the $2$-category $\mathrm{Cat}$ of categories, functors and natural transformations.
An equivalence in a $2$-category is a $1$-cell $F$ with a $1$-cell $G$ and invertible $2$-cells $GF\Rightarrow1$ and $FG\Rightarrow1$.
In $\mathrm{Cat}$, these data are a functor $F$, a functor $G$ and two natural isomorphisms, which is an equivalence of categories.
links.why: An equivalence of categories is the case of the general notion of equivalence in the $2$-category of categories.

steps: An adjoint equivalence is an adjunction $F\dashv G$ whose unit and counit are natural isomorphisms.
The adjunction also satisfies the triangle identities, but the next step does not need them.
Then $G$ is an inverse of $F$ up to natural isomorphism, so $F$ is an equivalence.
links.why: Every adjoint equivalence is an equivalence, and every equivalence can be improved to an adjoint equivalence.

reminder: A [module](c:module) is finitely generated when finitely many of its elements generate it.
definition: A left [module](c:module) $M$ over a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is finitely generated when there is a [finite set](c:finite-set) $\{m_1,\dots,m_n\}\subseteq M$ such that every element of $M$ equals $r_1m_1+\dots+r_nm_n$ for some $r_i\in R$. Equivalently, there is a [surjection](c:surjection) from a [free module](c:free-module) $R^n$ onto $M$.
examples: Every finite-dimensional vector space is finitely generated over its field, by any basis.
The ring $R$ is a finitely generated module over itself, generated by $1$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}$-module, because finitely many fractions have a common denominator $d$, and then $1/(2d)$ is not an integer combination of them.

steps: Start with a module $M$ over a ring $R$.
Ask for finitely many elements $m_1,\dots,m_n$ such that every element of $M$ is an $R$-combination of them.
A module that has such elements is finitely generated.
links.why: A finitely generated module is a module with a finite generating set, so all module theory applies to it.

steps: A finite-dimensional vector space $V$ over a field $k$ has a finite basis.
A basis spans $V$, so finitely many vectors generate $V$.
A vector space over $k$ is a $k$-module, so $V$ is a finitely generated $k$-module.
links.why: Results for finitely generated modules over a field are results about finite-dimensional vector spaces.

reminder: The flow of a [vector field](c:vector-field) moves each point along the integral curve of the field that starts at that point.
definition: Let $X$ be a smooth [vector field](c:vector-field) on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$. Its flow is the smooth map $\varphi(t,p)$, defined on an open set of $\mathbb{R}\times M$ that contains $\{0\}\times M$, with $\varphi(0,p)=p$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(t,p)=X(\varphi(t,p))$. When $\varphi$ is defined for all $t$, each $\varphi_t$ is a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) of $M$ and $\varphi_{s+t}=\varphi_s\circ\varphi_t$, so the maps $\varphi_t$ form a one-parameter [group](c:group).
examples: The field $X=x\,\partial_x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has the flow $\varphi_t(x)=e^tx$.
The rotation field $-y\,\partial_x+x\,\partial_y$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ has the rotation by the angle $t$ as its flow.
Non-example: the maps $\psi_t(x)=x+t^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ are not a flow, because $\psi_s\circ\psi_t\ne\psi_{s+t}$.

steps: A complete smooth vector field $X$ has a flow $\varphi_t$ defined for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
This flow satisfies $\varphi_0=\mathrm{id}$ and $\varphi_{s+t}=\varphi_s\circ\varphi_t$.
So $(t,p)\mapsto\varphi_t(p)$ is a continuous action of the additive monoid $\mathbb{R}$ on $M$.
links.why: The flow of a vector field is the main example of a flow, so results about general flows apply to it.

reminder: A fundamental domain is a measurable set whose translates under the group cover the space and overlap only in null sets.
definition: Let a [group](c:group) $G$ act on a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\mu)$ by a [group action](c:group-action). A fundamental domain is a [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $F\subseteq X$ such that the translates $gF$ for $g\in G$ cover $X$ up to a [null set](c:null-set), and $gF\cap hF$ is a null set whenever $g\ne h$.
examples: The interval $[0,1)$ is a fundamental domain for the group $\mathbb{Z}$ that acts on $\mathbb{R}$ by translation.
The square $[0,1)^2$ is a fundamental domain for $\mathbb{Z}^2$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with Lebesgue measure.
Non-example: $[0,2)$ is not a fundamental domain for $\mathbb{Z}$ acting on $\mathbb{R}$, because $[0,2)$ and its translate $1+[0,2)$ overlap in $[1,2)$, which is not null.

reminder: A Galois representation is a continuous [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) from an [absolute Galois group](c:absolute-galois-group) to $\mathrm{GL}_n$ of a topological ring.
definition: Let $K$ be a field and let $G_K=\mathrm{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{sep}}/K)$ be its [absolute Galois group](c:absolute-galois-group), with the profinite topology. An $n$-dimensional Galois representation over a [topological field](c:topological-field) or topological ring $E$, such as $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ or $\mathbb{F}_p$, is a continuous [group representation](c:group-representation) $\rho\colon G_K\to\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$ into the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) of $E$.
examples: The $\ell$-adic cyclotomic character $G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to\mathbb{Z}_\ell^\times$ records the action on the $\ell$-power roots of unity.
For an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, the action of $G_{\mathbb{Q}}$ on the $\ell$-adic Tate module of $E$ gives a $2$-dimensional representation over $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$.

Non-example: a homomorphism $G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ with infinite image is not continuous for the usual topology, because a profinite group maps continuously into $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ only with finite image.

steps: Take a group $G$ and a representation $\rho\colon G\to\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$.
Choose $G$ to be the absolute Galois group $G_K$ of a field $K$.
Choose $E$ to be a topological field or ring, and ask that $\rho$ is continuous for the profinite topology of $G_K$.
links.why: Every tool for group representations, such as characters and subrepresentations, applies to a Galois representation.

reminder: The greatest common divisor of two integers is the largest integer that divides both.
definition: For [integers](c:integer) $a$ and $b$ that are not both $0$, $\gcd(a,b)$ is the largest integer that divides both, in the sense of [divisibility](c:divisibility). Equivalently, it is the common divisor $d\ge0$ that every common divisor divides; in a [ring](c:ring), this second form defines a gcd, which is unique up to a unit.
examples: $\gcd(a,0)=|a|$ for every integer $a\ne0$.
Non-example: the number $3$ is a common divisor of $12$ and $18$ but not their gcd, because $6$ is a larger common divisor.

reminder: A homogeneous polynomial has all its [monomials](c:monomial) of the same degree.
definition: A [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is homogeneous of degree $d$ when every [monomial](c:monomial) of $f$ with a nonzero coefficient has total [degree](c:degree-of-a-polynomial) $d$. Over an infinite field this is equivalent to $f(\lambda x)=\lambda^d f(x)$ for all scalars $\lambda$.
examples: The polynomial $x^2+3xy-y^2$ is homogeneous of degree $2$.
The polynomial $x^3+y^3+z^3$ is homogeneous of degree $3$.
Non-example: $x^2+y$ is not homogeneous, because its monomials have the different degrees $2$ and $1$.

steps: Take a polynomial $f$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
Collect the monomials of $f$ that have a nonzero coefficient.
If all of them have the same total degree $d$, then $f$ is homogeneous of degree $d$.
links.why: Every fact about polynomials holds for homogeneous polynomials, and the degree condition makes projective geometry possible.

steps: Take a monomial $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ of total degree $d$.
Replace each $x_i$ by $\lambda x_i$, which multiplies the monomial by $\lambda^d$.
A sum of such monomials is also multiplied by $\lambda^d$, so $f(\lambda x)=\lambda^d f(x)$.
links.why: A homogeneous polynomial is a homogeneous function of integer degree, so scaling arguments apply to it.

reminder: A homotopy colimit is a [colimit](c:colimit) of a [diagram](c:diagram) that is computed in a way that respects [weak equivalences](c:weak-equivalence).
definition: For a [diagram](c:diagram) $D\colon I\to\mathcal{M}$ in a [model category](c:model-category) $\mathcal{M}$, the homotopy colimit $\operatorname{hocolim}D$ is the [colimit](c:colimit) of a cofibrant replacement of $D$, so it is the left derived functor of the colimit. It is invariant under [weak equivalences](c:weak-equivalence): if $D\to D'$ is a weak equivalence at each object of $I$, then $\operatorname{hocolim}D\to\operatorname{hocolim}D'$ is a weak equivalence.
examples: The homotopy pushout of $B\leftarrow A\to C$ is the double mapping cylinder, which replaces the plain pushout.
The homotopy colimit of a sequence $X_0\to X_1\to\cdots$ of spaces is its mapping telescope.
Non-example: the plain pushout of $*\leftarrow S^1\to*$ is a point, while the homotopy pushout is the suspension $S^2$, so the plain colimit is not homotopy invariant.

steps: Take the index category $I$ with objects $a$, $b$, $c$ and arrows $a\to b$ and $a\to c$.
A diagram of this shape is a span $B\leftarrow A\to C$.
The homotopy colimit of this span is the homotopy pushout.
links.why: Results about homotopy colimits apply to homotopy pushouts, the case of a span.

steps: Take the index category $\mathbb{N}$ with one arrow $n\to n+1$ for each $n$.
A diagram of this shape is a sequence $X_0\to X_1\to\cdots$.
The homotopy colimit of this sequence is its mapping telescope.
links.why: Results about homotopy colimits apply to mapping telescopes, the case of a sequence.

reminder: The homotopy group $\pi_n(X,x)$ is the group of homotopy classes of based maps from the $n$-sphere to $X$.
definition: For a [pointed space](c:pointed-space) $(X,x_0)$ and $n\ge1$, $\pi_n(X,x_0)$ is the set of classes, up to [homotopy](c:homotopy) that fixes the base point, of maps $(S^n,*)\to(X,x_0)$ from the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$. Its [group](c:group) operation joins two maps by pinching the equator of $S^n$, and for $n\ge2$ the group is abelian.
examples: $\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, where the integer counts how often a loop winds around the circle.
$\pi_n(\mathbb{R}^m)=0$ for all $n$, because $\mathbb{R}^m$ is contractible.
$\pi_2(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, where the integer is the degree of a map.
Non-example: the free homotopy classes of maps $S^1\to X$, without a base point, are not $\pi_1(X)$; they are the conjugacy classes of $\pi_1(X)$.

steps: Take $n=1$ in the definition of $\pi_n(X,x_0)$.
The sphere $S^1$ is the circle, so a based map $S^1\to X$ is a loop at $x_0$.
Homotopy classes of loops, with the operation of joining loops, form the fundamental group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$.
links.why: The fundamental group is the first homotopy group, so results for $\pi_n$ cover it.

reminder: The image of a [function](c:function) is the set of all values that the function takes.
definition: The image of a [function](c:function) $f\colon A\to B$ is the [subset](c:subset) $f(A)=\{f(a): a\in A\}$ of $B$. More generally, the image of a subset $S\subseteq A$ is $f(S)=\{f(a): a\in S\}$.
examples: For $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the image is $[0,\infty)$.
For $\sin\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, the image is $[-1,1]$.
Non-example: the codomain of $f$ is not its image unless $f$ is surjective; for $f(x)=x^2$ the codomain $\mathbb{R}$ is larger than the image $[0,\infty)$.

reminder: The induced representation builds a representation of $G$ from a representation of a subgroup $H$ by $k[G]\otimes_{k[H]}V$.
definition: Let $H$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of finite [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $m$ in a group $G$, and let $V$ be a [representation](c:group-representation) of $H$ over a field $k$. The induced representation is $\operatorname{Ind}_H^GV=k[G]\otimes_{k[H]}V$, the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) of $V$ with the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) $k[G]$ over $k[H]$, where $G$ acts by left multiplication on $k[G]$. Its dimension is $m\dim V$.
examples: Inducing the trivial representation of $H$ gives the permutation representation of $G$ on the cosets $G/H$.
Inducing from the trivial subgroup $\{1\}$ gives the regular representation of $G$.
Non-example: the restriction of a representation of $G$ to $H$ goes the other way, from $G$ to $H$, so it is not an induced representation.

steps: Take the trivial representation $k$ of $H$.
Then $k[G]\otimes_{k[H]}k$ has the cosets $gH$ as a basis.
The group $G$ permutes these cosets by left multiplication, which gives the permutation representation on $G/H$.
links.why: A permutation representation on cosets is an induced representation, so results on induction cover it.

reminder: An integral domain is a nonzero [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) in which a product of nonzero elements is never zero.
definition: An integral domain is a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors: if $ab=0$ then $a=0$ or $b=0$. Equivalently, nonzero elements can be cancelled: $ac=bc$ and $c\ne0$ imply $a=b$.
examples: The ring $\mathbb{Z}$ of integers and every field are integral domains.
The polynomial ring $k[x]$ over a field $k$ is an integral domain.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/6$ is not an integral domain, because $2\cdot3=0$ while $2\ne0$ and $3\ne0$.

steps: Start with a commutative ring $R$.
Require $1\ne0$ in $R$.
Require that $ab=0$ implies $a=0$ or $b=0$.
links.why: Every fact about commutative rings holds for integral domains, which add the cancellation law.

steps: A field $F$ is a commutative ring with $1\ne0$ in which every nonzero element has an inverse.
Suppose $ab=0$ in $F$ with $a\ne0$.
Multiply by $a^{-1}$ to get $b=0$, so $F$ has no zero divisors and is an integral domain.
links.why: Results for integral domains, such as the existence of a field of fractions, apply to every field.

steps: A principal ideal domain is an integral domain in which every ideal has one generator.
The first part of this definition is the definition of an integral domain.
Drop the condition on ideals, and an integral domain remains.
links.why: Results for integral domains apply to principal ideal domains.

reminder: An element $a$ of a [monoid](c:monoid) is invertible when some element $b$ satisfies $ab=1$ and $ba=1$.
definition: An element $a$ of a [monoid](c:monoid), such as a ring under multiplication, is invertible when there is an element $b$ with $ab=1=ba$. This $b$ is unique, it is written $a^{-1}$, and the invertible elements form a [group](c:group), the [group of units](c:group-of-units).
examples: In the ring $\mathbb{Z}$, the invertible elements are exactly $1$ and $-1$.
A square matrix over a field is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.
Non-example: $2$ is not invertible in $\mathbb{Z}$, because no integer $b$ has $2b=1$, although $2$ is invertible in $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps: View the monoid $M$ as a category with one object and the elements of $M$ as arrows.
An arrow $a$ is an isomorphism when some arrow $b$ has $ab=1$ and $ba=1$.
So $a$ is an invertible element exactly when $a$ is an isomorphism of this category.
links.why: An invertible element is an isomorphism in a one-object category, so results on isomorphisms apply to it.

steps: View the monoid $M$ as a discrete monoidal category, with the elements as objects and the product as tensor product.
An object $a$ is invertible when some object $b$ has $a\otimes b\cong1\cong b\otimes a$.
In a discrete category, isomorphic objects are equal, so $a$ is an invertible object exactly when $ab=1=ba$.
links.why: An invertible element is an invertible object of a discrete monoidal category.

reminder: The Jacobian determinant of a differentiable map from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the [determinant](c:determinant) of its matrix of partial derivatives.
definition: For a [differentiable function](c:differentiable-function) $f=(f_1,\dots,f_n)$ from an open set of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$, the Jacobian determinant at $x$ is $J_f(x)=\det\big(\partial f_i/\partial x_j(x)\big)$, the [determinant](c:determinant) of the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix). Its absolute value is the factor by which $f$ scales volume near $x$, and its sign tells whether $f$ keeps orientation.
examples: The polar map $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ has the Jacobian determinant $r$.
A linear map $x\mapsto Ax$ has the constant Jacobian determinant $\det A$.
Non-example: a map $\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^3$ has a $3\times2$ Jacobian matrix, which is not square, so it has no Jacobian determinant.

reminder: The Laplace transform of $f$ is the function $F(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt$ of the complex variable $s$.
definition: For a locally integrable [function](c:function) $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{C}$, the Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}f(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt$, defined for those [complex numbers](c:complex-number) $s$ at which this [integral](c:integral) converges. It turns differentiation into multiplication: $\mathcal{L}(f')(s)=s\,\mathcal{L}f(s)-f(0)$ when both sides exist.
examples: $\mathcal{L}\{1\}(s)=1/s$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>0$.
$\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\}(s)=1/(s-a)$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>\operatorname{Re}a$.
Non-example: for $f(t)=e^{t^2}$ the integral $\int_0^\infty e^{-st}e^{t^2}\,dt$ diverges for every $s$, so $f$ has no Laplace transform.

steps: Take a function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $f(t)=0$ for $t<0$.
Put $s=i\omega$ with $\omega$ real.
Then $\int_0^\infty e^{-i\omega t}f(t)\,dt$ is the Fourier transform of $f$, whenever the integral converges.
links.why: On the imaginary axis, the Laplace transform of a function on the half line is its Fourier transform, so Fourier tools carry over.

steps: The Fourier-Laplace transform integrates $f(x)e^{-ax}$ over an affine space, for a complex parameter $a$.
Take the affine space $\mathbb{R}$ and a function $f$ that is supported on $[0,\infty)$.
The resulting integral is the Laplace transform of $f$ at $s=a$.
links.why: The Laplace transform and the Fourier transform are two cases of one transform, which unifies their rules.

reminder: The Lefschetz number of a map $f\colon X\to X$ is the alternating sum of the traces of $f_*$ on rational homology.
definition: Let $X$ be a [compact](c:compact-space) triangulable space and $f\colon X\to X$ a [continuous map](c:continuous-function). The Lefschetz number is $L(f)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\operatorname{tr}\big(f_*\mid H_k(X;\mathbb{Q})\big)$, the alternating sum of the [traces](c:trace-of-a-matrix) of the maps that $f$ induces on [homology](c:homology). The sum is finite, because only finitely many $H_k(X;\mathbb{Q})$ are nonzero and each has finite dimension.
examples: For $f=\mathrm{id}_X$, the Lefschetz number $L(f)$ is the Euler characteristic $\chi(X)$.
A constant map on a connected space has $L(f)=1$, because it acts as the identity on $H_0$ and as zero on $H_k$ for $k>0$.
Non-example: the unsigned sum of traces is not the Lefschetz number; for $\mathrm{id}$ on $S^1$ it is $1+1=2$, but $L(\mathrm{id})=1-1=0$.

steps: Take $f$ to be the identity map $\mathrm{id}_X$ of the space $X$.
Then $f_*$ is the identity on each $H_k(X;\mathbb{Q})$, and the trace of an identity map is the dimension.
So $L(\mathrm{id}_X)=\sum_k(-1)^k\dim H_k(X;\mathbb{Q})$, which is the Euler characteristic $\chi(X)$.
links.why: The Euler characteristic is the Lefschetz number of the identity, so fixed point arguments extend it to all maps.

reminder: A Lie bracket is a [bilinear map](c:bilinear-map) that is antisymmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity.
definition: A Lie bracket on a vector space $\mathfrak{g}$ is a [bilinear map](c:bilinear-map) $[\cdot,\cdot]\colon\mathfrak{g}\times\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{g}$ with $[x,x]=0$ and $[x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]]=0$ for all $x,y,z$. With this bracket, $\mathfrak{g}$ is a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra). For [vector fields](c:vector-field) $X$ and $Y$, the bracket is $[X,Y]f=X(Yf)-Y(Xf)$.
examples: The commutator $[A,B]=AB-BA$ of $n\times n$ matrices.
The bracket of vector fields on $\mathbb{R}$, for example $[x\,\partial_x,\partial_x]=-\partial_x$.
Non-example: the anticommutator $AB+BA$ of matrices is bilinear but symmetric, and $A\cdot A+A\cdot A=2A^2\ne0$ in general, so it is not a Lie bracket.

steps: In an associative algebra $A$, set $[a,b]=ab-ba$.
This map is bilinear, and $[a,a]=aa-aa=0$.
A direct expansion shows the Jacobi identity, so the commutator is a Lie bracket on $A$.
links.why: Every associative algebra gives a Lie algebra, and the Lie bracket axioms record what the commutator satisfies.

steps: A Poisson bracket $\{f,g\}$ on smooth functions is bilinear and antisymmetric, so $\{f,f\}=0$.
It also satisfies the Jacobi identity.
So the Poisson bracket is a Lie bracket on the vector space of smooth functions.
links.why: Results about Lie brackets apply to Poisson brackets.

reminder: A [category](c:category) is locally small when each collection of morphisms between two objects is a set.
definition: A [category](c:category) $C$ is locally small when, for all objects $x$ and $y$, the collection $C(x,y)$ of morphisms from $x$ to $y$ is a [small set](c:small-set), not a proper class. In this case each $C(x,y)$ is a [hom-set](c:hom-set), and the hom-functors of $C$ take values in the category of sets.
examples: The category of sets and functions is locally small, although it has a proper class of objects.
Every small category is locally small.
Non-example: the one-object category whose morphisms are all ordinals, composed by ordinal addition, is not locally small, because its only hom-collection is a proper class.

steps: Start with any category $C$.
Ask that every collection of morphisms $C(x,y)$ is a set.
A category that meets this condition is locally small.
links.why: Every fact about categories holds for locally small categories, which also have hom-functors into sets.

steps: A small category has a set of objects and a set of morphisms.
Each collection $C(x,y)$ is a subset of the set of all morphisms, so it is a set.
So a small category is locally small.
links.why: Results for locally small categories apply to small categories.

reminder: A measurable space is a [set](c:set) together with a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) of subsets that count as measurable.
definition: A measurable space is a pair $(X,\mathcal{A})$ of a [set](c:set) $X$ and a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal{A}$ on $X$: a family of subsets of $X$ that contains $X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions. The members of $\mathcal{A}$ are the [measurable sets](c:measurable-set).
examples: The real line $\mathbb{R}$ with the $\sigma$-algebra of Borel sets.
Any set $X$ with its power set, or with the trivial $\sigma$-algebra $\{\varnothing,X\}$.
Non-example: the finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ do not form a $\sigma$-algebra, because the complement of a finite set is infinite and so is not in the family.

steps: Take a measure space $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$.
Forget the measure $\mu$ and keep the pair $(X,\mathcal{A})$.
The pair is a measurable space, so every measure space has an underlying measurable space.
links.why: Notions that do not use the measure, such as measurable functions, live on the measurable space.

steps: Take a [Polish space](c:polish-space) $P$ and its Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}(P)$.
The pair $(P,\mathcal{B}(P))$ is a measurable space.
A measurable space that is isomorphic to such a pair is a standard Borel space, which adds the condition of coming from a Polish topology.
links.why: Results for measurable spaces apply to standard Borel spaces, which have extra tools such as the isomorphism theorem.

reminder: A measure-preserving map $T$ satisfies $\mu(T^{-1}(B))=\nu(B)$ for every measurable set $B$ of the target.
definition: Let $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B},\nu)$ be [measure spaces](c:measure-space). A [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $T\colon X\to Y$ is measure preserving when $\mu(T^{-1}(B))=\nu(B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal{B}$, where $T^{-1}(B)$ is the [preimage](c:preimage) of $B$.
examples: The rotation $x\mapsto x+\alpha\bmod1$ on $[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure.
The doubling map $x\mapsto2x\bmod1$ with Lebesgue measure, because the preimage of an interval is two intervals of half the length.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x/2$ from $[0,1)$ to $[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure, because the preimage of $[0,1/2)$ is $[0,1)$, which has measure $1$ and not $1/2$.

steps: Take a measurable function $T\colon X\to Y$ between measure spaces.
Compare $\mu(T^{-1}(B))$ with $\nu(B)$ for each measurable set $B$.
If they are equal for every $B$, then $T$ preserves the measure.
links.why: Every fact about measurable functions holds for measure-preserving maps, which add the equality of measures.

reminder: Modus ponens is the rule that gives $Q$ from the two premises $P$ and $P\to Q$.
definition: Modus ponens is the inference rule that, from a proof of $P$ and a proof of the [implication](c:implication) $P\to Q$, gives a proof of $Q$. It is the elimination rule for $\to$ among the [logical connectives](c:logical-connective).
examples: From $x>0$ and the implication $x>0\to x^2>0$, modus ponens gives $x^2>0$.
From 'it rains' and 'if it rains, the street is wet', modus ponens gives 'the street is wet'.
Non-example: from $Q$ and $P\to Q$, the conclusion $P$ does not follow; this error is called affirming the consequent.

reminder: An ordinary differential equation relates an unknown [function](c:function) of one variable to its [derivatives](c:derivative).
definition: An ordinary differential equation of order $n$ is an equation $F(t,y,y',\dots,y^{(n)})=0$ for an unknown [function](c:function) $y$ of one real variable $t$. A solution is an $n$ times differentiable $y$ on an interval that satisfies the equation, where $y',y'',\dots$ are the [derivatives](c:derivative) of $y$.
examples: The equation $y'=y$ has the solutions $y=Ce^t$.
The equation $y''+y=0$ has the solutions $y=a\cos t+b\sin t$.
Non-example: the heat equation $u_t=u_{xx}$ has derivatives in two variables, so it is a partial differential equation and not an ordinary one.

steps: A differential equation relates an unknown function to its derivatives.
Restrict to unknown functions of one variable.
Then every derivative is an ordinary derivative, and the equation is an ordinary differential equation.
links.why: Every fact about differential equations holds for ordinary ones, which add the one-variable setting and its existence theorems.

steps: A Riccati equation has the form $y'=q_0(t)+q_1(t)y+q_2(t)y^2$.
It relates the unknown function $y$ of one variable to its first derivative.
So it is a first-order ordinary differential equation with a quadratic right side.
links.why: Results for ordinary differential equations, such as existence and uniqueness, apply to Riccati equations.

reminder: An orthonormal set is a set of vectors that are pairwise [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) and each have length one.
definition: In an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) $V$, a set $S\subseteq V$ is orthonormal when $\langle u,v\rangle=0$ for all different $u,v\in S$ and $\langle u,u\rangle=1$ for all $u\in S$. In other words, the vectors of $S$ are pairwise [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) [unit vectors](c:unit-vector).
examples: The standard basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product.
The functions $e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ in $L^2([0,2\pi])$.
Non-example: $\{(1,0),(1,1)\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not orthonormal, because the vectors are not orthogonal and $(1,1)$ has length $\sqrt2$.

steps: An orthonormal basis is an orthonormal set whose span is dense in the space.
Forget the condition on the span.
What remains is an orthonormal set.
links.why: Facts about orthonormal sets, such as Bessel's inequality, apply to every orthonormal basis.

reminder: Parallel lines are distinct [lines](c:line) in one [plane](c:plane) that have no common point.
definition: Two distinct [lines](c:line) in a [plane](c:plane) are parallel when they have no common point. Equivalently, in the Euclidean plane, one line is the image of the other under a [translation](c:translation).
examples: The lines $y=2x$ and $y=2x+3$ are parallel, because they have the same slope and different intercepts.
Opposite sides of a parallelogram lie on parallel lines.
Non-example: two lines in space that do not meet and do not lie in one plane are skew lines, not parallel lines.

reminder: A [function](c:function) $f$ is periodic when $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x$ and some fixed $p>0$.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ is periodic when there is a [period](c:period) $p>0$ with $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all real $x$. Then $f(x+np)=f(x)$ for every integer $n$, so the graph repeats on each interval of length $p$.
examples: The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ have the period $2\pi$.
The fractional part $x-\lfloor x\rfloor$ has the period $1$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto e^x$ is not periodic on $\mathbb{R}$, because it is strictly increasing, so $e^{x+p}\ne e^x$ for $p>0$.

reminder: A Polish space is a [separable](c:separable-space) [topological space](c:topological-space) whose topology comes from a [complete metric](c:complete-metric-space).
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is Polish when it is [separable](c:separable-space) and there is a [complete metric](c:complete-metric-space) on $X$ that induces its topology. In other words, $X$ is homeomorphic to a separable complete metric space.
examples: The real line $\mathbb{R}$, and more generally $\mathbb{R}^n$ and the separable Hilbert space $\ell^2$.
Every compact metric space, such as the Cantor space, is Polish.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ with its usual topology is not Polish, because a countable space with no isolated points cannot be completely metrizable, by the Baire category theorem.

steps: Take a compact metric space $K$.
It is complete, since a Cauchy sequence has a convergent subsequence and therefore converges.
It is separable, because for each $n$ finitely many balls of radius $1/n$ cover $K$, and their centres form a countable dense set.
So $K$ is separable and completely metrizable, hence Polish.
links.why: Results for Polish spaces apply to every compact metric space.

steps: Take a separable Banach space $E$ with the norm metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$.
This metric is complete, because $E$ is a Banach space.
The space $E$ is separable by assumption.
So $E$ is separable and completely metrizable, hence Polish.
links.why: Results for Polish spaces apply to every separable Banach space.

reminder: A probability density function $f$ of a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ satisfies $P(X\in A)=\int_A f\,dx$ for every Borel set $A$.
definition: A [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a probability density function $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to[0,\infty)$ when $f$ is measurable and $P(X\in A)=\int_A f\,d\lambda$ for every Borel set $A$, where $\lambda$ is [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) and the [integral](c:integral) is taken over $A$. Then $\int f\,d\lambda=1$, and $f$ is the [Radon-Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) of the law of $X$ with respect to $\lambda$.
examples: The standard normal density $f(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$.
The uniform density $f=\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$ on $[0,1]$.
Non-example: a fair coin toss $X\in\{0,1\}$ has no density, because $P(X=0)=1/2$ but the integral of any function over the single point $\{0\}$ is $0$.

steps: Take a random variable $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its law $P_X$, a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Suppose $P_X$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure $\lambda$.
Then the Radon-Nikodym derivative $dP_X/d\lambda$ exists, and it is a density of $X$.
links.why: A density is a Radon-Nikodym derivative with respect to Lebesgue measure, so the Radon-Nikodym theorem shows when densities exist.

reminder: A rational function is a quotient of two [polynomials](c:polynomial) whose denominator is not zero.
definition: A rational function over a [field](c:field) $k$ is a quotient $p/q$ of two [polynomials](c:polynomial) $p,q$ over $k$ with $q\ne0$, where $p/q$ and $p'/q'$ are equal when $pq'=p'q$. The rational functions form the [field of fractions](c:field-of-fractions) $k(x)$ of the polynomial ring $k[x]$.
examples: The quotient $(x^2+1)/(x-3)$ is a rational function.
Every polynomial $p$ is the rational function $p/1$.
Non-example: $\sqrt{x}$ is not a rational function, because $p^2=xq^2$ has no polynomial solutions with $q\ne0$, as the two sides have degrees of different parity.

steps: A polynomial $p$ equals the quotient $p/1$.
The denominator $1$ is a nonzero polynomial.
So every polynomial is a rational function.
links.why: Results for rational functions apply to polynomials as the case of denominator one.

steps: Take a rational function $p/q$ over $\mathbb{C}$ with $q\ne0$.
At each point where $q\ne0$, the quotient $p/q$ is holomorphic.
At each zero of $q$, it has a pole or a removable singularity, so $p/q$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb{C}$.
links.why: Rational functions are the simplest meromorphic functions, so the tools of complex analysis apply to them.

reminder: Robinson arithmetic is a finite first-order theory of the natural numbers that has no induction axioms.
definition: Robinson arithmetic $Q$ is the [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) in the [signature](c:signature-in-logic) $\{0,S,+,\cdot\}$ with the axioms $Sx\ne0$, $Sx=Sy\to x=y$, $x\ne0\to\exists y\,(x=Sy)$, $x+0=x$, $x+Sy=S(x+y)$, $x\cdot0=0$ and $x\cdot Sy=x\cdot y+x$. It is [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic) with the induction schema removed.
examples: The natural numbers with the usual successor, sum and product satisfy all seven axioms.
$Q$ proves $S0+S0=SS0$, by one use of $x+Sy=S(x+y)$ and one use of $x+0=x$.
Non-example: the integers with $S(x)=x+1$ are not a model of $Q$, because $S(-1)=0$ breaks the axiom $Sx\ne0$.
Non-example: $Q$ does not prove $\forall x\,(0+x=x)$, which is true in $\mathbb{N}$ but needs induction.

steps: Every axiom of $Q$ is a theorem of Peano arithmetic.
So every model of Peano arithmetic is a model of $Q$.
Peano arithmetic adds the induction schema to $Q$, which shrinks the class of models.
links.why: A result proved from $Q$ alone holds in every model of Peano arithmetic.

reminder: A scheme is a [locally ringed space](c:locally-ringed-space) that is locally the [prime spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring).
definition: A scheme is a [locally ringed space](c:locally-ringed-space) $(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ with an open cover by sets $U_i$ such that each $(U_i,\mathcal{O}_X|_{U_i})$ is isomorphic to the [prime spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) $\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $A_i$, with its structure [sheaf](c:sheaf). A morphism of schemes is a morphism of locally ringed spaces.
examples: The prime spectrum $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$, and in general every affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A$.
Projective space $\mathbb{P}^n_k$, glued from $n+1$ copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$.
Non-example: an open interval of $\mathbb{R}$ with its sheaf of smooth functions is a locally ringed space but not a scheme, because it is not locally the spectrum of a ring.

steps: Start with a locally ringed space $(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$.
Ask for an open cover of $X$ by pieces $U_i$.
Require each piece, with its restricted sheaf, to be isomorphic to $\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ for a commutative ring $A_i$.
links.why: Every fact about locally ringed spaces holds for schemes, which add the local ring spectrum condition.

steps: Take a variety $X$ over an algebraically closed field $k$, covered by affine varieties with coordinate rings $A_i$.
Each $A_i$ is a commutative ring.
Glue the spectra $\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ along the same overlaps to get a scheme.
links.why: Scheme theory covers varieties and also spaces over rings that are not fields.

steps: An affine scheme is $\operatorname{Spec}A$ for a commutative ring $A$.
Cover $\operatorname{Spec}A$ by the single open set $\operatorname{Spec}A$ itself.
This cover shows that $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is locally a spectrum, so it is a scheme.
links.why: Results for schemes apply to affine schemes, the building blocks of every scheme.

reminder: The signature of a real symmetric bilinear form is the number of positive squares minus the number of negative squares.
definition: The signature of a nondegenerate symmetric [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $B$ on a finite-dimensional real vector space is $p-q$, where $B(x,x)=x_1^2+\dots+x_p^2-x_{p+1}^2-\dots-x_{p+q}^2$ in a suitable basis. The numbers $p$ and $q$ do not depend on the basis, by Sylvester's law of inertia. The signature of a closed oriented [manifold](c:manifold) of dimension $4k$ is the signature of its [intersection form](c:intersection-form) on $H^{2k}(M;\mathbb{R})$.
examples: The form $x_1^2-x_2^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ has $p=q=1$, so its signature is $0$.
The complex projective plane $\mathbb{CP}^2$ has the intersection form $(1)$, so its signature is $1$.
Non-example: the torus $T^2$ has dimension $2$, so its intersection form on $H^1$ is skew-symmetric and has no signature in this sense.

steps: Take a pseudo-Riemannian metric $g$ on a manifold and a point $x$.
The value $g_x$ is a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on the tangent space at $x$.
The signature of the metric is the signature of this form.
links.why: Facts about the signature of a form, such as Sylvester's law, apply to metrics point by point.

reminder: A signed measure is a countably additive set function on a sigma-algebra that may take negative values.
definition: A signed measure on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $(X,\mathcal{A})$ is a function $\mu\colon\mathcal{A}\to(-\infty,\infty]$, or into $[-\infty,\infty)$, with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ that is countably additive: $\mu\big(\bigsqcup_nA_n\big)=\sum_n\mu(A_n)$ for pairwise disjoint sets $A_n\in\mathcal{A}$. Unlike a [measure](c:measure), it may take negative values, and it is finite when it takes only real values.
examples: For an integrable function $f$ that changes sign, $A\mapsto\int_Af\,d\lambda$ is a signed measure.
The difference $\mu_1-\mu_2$ of two finite measures is a signed measure.
Non-example: $A\mapsto\lambda(A)^2$ on Lebesgue measurable sets is not a signed measure, because it is not additive: two disjoint unit intervals give $4\ne1+1$.

steps: Take a measure $\mu\colon\mathcal{A}\to[0,\infty]$.
It satisfies $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ and is countably additive.
Its values lie in $(-\infty,\infty]$, so $\mu$ is a signed measure that has no negative values.
links.why: Results for signed measures apply to ordinary measures as the case without negative values.

steps: A vector measure is a countably additive function on a $\sigma$-algebra with values in an additive monoid $M$.
Take $M=\mathbb{R}$ and a finite signed measure $\mu$.
The map $\mu$ is countably additive and sends $\varnothing$ to $0$, so it is a vector measure.
links.why: A finite signed measure is a real vector measure, so results on vector measures apply to it.

reminder: A simple closed curve is a subset of a space that is [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to a [circle](c:circle).
definition: A simple closed curve in a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a subset $C\subseteq X$ that is [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to the [circle](c:circle) $S^1$. In a Hausdorff space, this means that $C$ is the image of a [continuous map](c:continuous-function) $\gamma\colon[0,1]\to X$ with $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)$ that is injective on $[0,1)$.
examples: A round circle or an ellipse in the plane.
The boundary of a square in the plane.
Non-example: the figure eight is not a simple closed curve, because a loop that traces it passes the crossing point twice.

steps: A closed curve is a continuous map $\gamma\colon[0,1]\to X$ with $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)$.
Require $\gamma$ to be injective on $[0,1)$, so that the curve never crosses itself.
In a Hausdorff space, the image of such a map is homeomorphic to $S^1$, so it is a simple closed curve.
links.why: A simple closed curve is a closed curve without self-crossings, so facts about closed curves apply.

steps: Take a round circle $C$ of radius $r$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
Scaling and translating gives a homeomorphism between $C$ and the unit circle $S^1$.
So $C$ is homeomorphic to $S^1$, which makes it a simple closed curve.
links.why: Every theorem about simple closed curves applies to round circles.

reminder: A simply connected [manifold](c:manifold) is a connected manifold in which every loop can shrink to a point.
definition: A [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ is simply connected when it is [path connected](c:path-connected-space) and its [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(M)$ is the [trivial group](c:trivial-group). Equivalently, every loop in $M$ can be continuously contracted to a point.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ for $n\ge2$, and Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is simply connected.
Non-example: the circle $S^1$ is not simply connected, because a loop that goes once around it cannot shrink; its fundamental group is $\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: the torus $T^2$ is not simply connected, because its fundamental group is $\mathbb{Z}^2$.

steps: Start with a simply connected space $X$, which is path connected and has a trivial fundamental group.
Add the condition that $X$ is a manifold.
The result is a simply connected manifold.
links.why: Every fact about simply connected spaces, such as lifting criteria for covering maps, applies to these manifolds.

steps: Start with a manifold $M$.
Require that $M$ is path connected.
Require that every loop in $M$ shrinks to a point, which means that $\pi_1(M)$ is trivial.
links.why: Every fact about manifolds holds for simply connected manifolds, which add a topological condition.
